title: Understanding KV Caching in LLM Inference (A Practical, Intuitive Guide)
author: Anurag Mohan

blocks.text: Let’s build an intuition for KV caching step by step, starting from the core problem and gradually arriving at why caching is necessary—and what tradeoffs it introduces.
Why Computation Becomes Expensive Without Caching
Consider a simple input:
"The cat sat"
The model processes this and generates the next word:
"on"
Now the input becomes:
"The cat sat on"
Here is the key issue:
Without any optimization, the model recomputes everything from scratch at every step.
That means:

It reprocesses "The"
It reprocesses "cat"
It reprocesses "sat"
Then processes "on"
This happens because of how attention works.
How Attention Drives This Cost
Inside the model, each word looks at every other word to understand context.
For a sentence like:
"The cat sat"
Each word interacts with all others:

"The" looks at "cat" and "sat"
"cat" looks at "The" and "sat"
"sat" looks at "The" and "cat"
As the sentence grows longer, the amount of work increases rapidly.
If there are n words, the number of interactions is proportional to n × n.
Now combine this with generation:

Step 1: process 3 words → ~9 interactions
Step 2: process 4 words → ~16 interactions
Step 3: process 5 words → ~25 interactions
This leads to a growing amount of repeated computation.
The Core Idea Behind KV Caching
Instead of recomputing everything, we store intermediate results and reuse them.
Inside each layer of the model, for every word, two important vectors are created:

A key vector (used to determine relevance)
A value vector (used to carry information)
KV caching means:
Store these vectors so they can be reused when new words are generated.
What Exactly Is Being Stored?
Let’s define the components clearly.
A vector is simply a list of numbers, for example:
A layer is one stage of processing. Models typically have many layers, and each word is processed through all of them.
For every word and every layer, we store:

one key vector
one value vector
Building a Simple Example
Assume:

1 sentence
3 words: "The cat sat"
2 layers
For each layer:
Each word produces a key vector and a value vector
So for one layer:
3 words × 2 vectors = 6 vectors
For two layers:
2 × 6 = 12 vectors
What Happens When a New Word Is Added?
Now the sentence becomes:
"The cat sat on"
We only compute vectors for the new word.
For that new word:

Layer 1 → key + value
Layer 2 → key + value
So we add:
2 layers × 2 vectors = 4 vectors
The previously computed vectors are reused.
Why This Improves Performance
With KV caching:

Previously computed key and value vectors are reused
Only the new word is processed
This changes the cost of generation significantly.
Without caching:
Each step recomputes everything → grows rapidly
With caching:
Each step processes only the new word → grows linearly
The Memory Tradeoff
The improvement in speed comes at the cost of memory.
All stored key and value vectors must remain in memory during generation.
Where Is This Data Stored?
KV cache is stored in GPU memory (also called VRAM).
This is the same memory used for:

model weights
intermediate computations
It is stored on the GPU because:

the model runs on the GPU
accessing GPU memory is much faster than transferring data from CPU memory
Why Memory Becomes a Bottleneck
Let’s scale the earlier example.
Assume:

32 layers
1000 words
each vector contains 4096 numbers
Total vectors:
32 layers × 1000 words × 2 (key and value) = 64,000 vectors
Total numbers:
64,000 × 4096 ≈ 262 million numbers
If each number takes 2 bytes of memory:
≈ 524 MB for a single user
With multiple users, memory usage grows proportionally.
Intuition for Memory Growth
For every new word:

new key and value vectors are added
across all layers
This means memory grows linearly with:

number of words
number of layers
number of users
Putting It All Together
KV caching introduces a fundamental tradeoff:

Faster generation by avoiding repeated computation
Increased memory usage due to storing intermediate results
What Comes Next
As systems scale, memory becomes the primary constraint rather than computation.
This leads to the next set of questions:

How do we manage GPU memory efficiently?
How do we serve many users simultaneously?
How do we reduce the size of the KV cache?
These questions lead to techniques such as:

paged attention
prefix caching
quantization
memory offloading
We will explore these in the next part.
Summary

KV caching improves inference speed by storing key and value vectors for each word at every layer, avoiding recomputation. However, this shifts the bottleneck from computation to memory, making efficient memory management critical in real-world systems.
